stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object

Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# ARC panel marker-count classification

Use when an ARC input has a repeated rectangular grid of panels separated by full-color divider rows/columns, sparse marker cells inside panels, and a smaller output matrix aligned to the panels.

## Procedure
1. Identify full horizontal/vertical divider lines and partition the input into panels, excluding divider cells.
2. For each panel, count cells of the unusual marker color(s), not the separator or base colors.
3. Use all current-instance demo pairs to map each marker count/panel feature to its output value. Verify every output cell; specifically check panels with distinct counts.
4. Apply that mapping to each test panel, with output dimensions equal to the number of panel rows/columns.
5. Validate every output row length and preserve the evidenced fallback value for unobserved counts.

## Solved example and caution

# Sparse diagonal stroke continuation

## When to use
Use when an ARC grid has a mostly uniform background and compact sparse motifs that may encode diagonal lines extended to grid boundaries. This is a class-level hypothesis workflow, not an ID-specific answer recipe.

## Workflow
1. Record all non-background coordinates and group by color. Separate same-color aligned pairs/segments from isolated cells and from mixed-color diagonal chains.
2. For each plausible same-color segment, test both diagonal orientations (down-right/up-left and down-left/up-right). Identify segment endpoints and compute exact ray cells to boundaries without altering the seed.
3. Compare each prediction against every demo output. Record which colors/segments extend, which directions fire, and which plausible near-matches are unchanged. Do not infer that every diagonal pair activates.
4. Apply only the demonstrated selector and ray paths to the test. Preserve other cells and seed colors unless outputs explicitly change them. Mechanically validate dimensions and coordinate indices.
5. After incorrect feedback, reject that hypothesis and identify the alternative selector distinction; do not repeat a similar output with minor transcription changes.

## Pitfalls
- Mixed-color objects can resemble a diagonal run; require same-color evidence unless demos show otherwise.
- Extending all same-color diagonal segments is not established merely because one demo extends a pair. A test submission extending both a 9 diagonal pair and a separate 1 pair was rejected. Selector behavior was not fully revealed.
- Examples show variable direction and palette: a color-6 diagonal seed extended up-left to the top boundary, a color-7 seed extended down-left to the bottom, and a color-9 pair extended down-left. Derive direction per instance.
- Stroke endpoints may already contain multiple seed cells; preserve every original seed cell and extend outward from the correct endpoint rather than overwriting or filling the whole diagonal indiscriminately.

## Evidence scope
Task-4fbd50f1 supplied three demos and two incorrect test submissions. Demos support diagonal stroke extensions, but do not determine the correct test output: a candidate extending two plausible segments was rejected. This is partial evidence only, not a validated complete rule.
